vignette:
The Weight of What He Carried Back

Marcus is twenty-nine years old and works alone most days at a small jewelry bench in the back of a shop his uncle owns in Portland, Oregon. He likes the precision of the work — the way a loupe brings the world down to something tiny and manageable, something he can hold still with his fingers. He chose to come back to the bench after everything. He says it's the only place where his hands don't shake.

Three years ago, Marcus spent eight months in a conflict zone in eastern Syria as a volunteer relief worker with a humanitarian aid organization. He had gone with idealism and a duffel bag, twenty-six years old and certain that showing up was the most important thing a person could do. For the first few months, that belief held. He distributed food, helped coordinate medical supply chains, translated when he could, and slept in shared quarters with a rotating cast of workers from a dozen countries. He felt useful. He felt, for the first time in his life, that he was exactly where he was supposed to be.

Then came the morning in February when a convoy he was supposed to be traveling in was struck. He had stayed behind at the distribution point because of a logistical dispute over paperwork — a decision that felt meaningless at the time and now feels like the hinge on which his entire life swings. Three of his colleagues were killed. A fourth, a woman named Dara who had become his closest friend there, lost her left hand and most of her hearing. Marcus was the one who reached her first. He remembers the color of the dust and the particular sound the air made, a kind of pressure-filled silence, before the noise came back all at once.

He finished his deployment. He doesn't fully understand why. He came home to Portland in the fall, thinner, quieter, and unable to explain to his family what had happened in any way that felt honest. He started back at the jewelry bench within weeks, telling himself that routine was recovery.

It isn't. At night, Marcus rarely sleeps more than three or four hours before something pulls him back to the surface — a sound, a dream, or sometimes nothing at all, just a sudden and absolute certainty that something terrible is about to happen. He lies in the dark and runs through the logistics of that February morning the way he once ran supply inventories, looking for the variable he missed, the decision that could have saved them. He has never found one, and the searching itself has become its own kind of torment.

During the day, he moves through the world with a hypervigilance that exhausts him. He sits with his back to walls in restaurants, rarely goes to restaurants at all anymore, and has stopped seeing most of his friends because the effort of appearing normal has become more than he can sustain. He has unfollowed every news account on his phone. He cannot watch footage of any kind of explosion or emergency, even in fiction — his body responds before his mind can intervene, heart slamming, vision narrowing, hands going cold.

What troubles Marcus most, and what he speaks about with a particular kind of grief, is that he no longer feels the idealism that sent him there. He describes it as an amputation. He wanted to care about the world and the world showed him exactly what it was, and now he sits at a small bench in Portland and sets tiny stones into precious metal and tries to find something in the smallness of that work that feels like enough.

He still emails Dara occasionally. She has rebuilt her life in Amsterdam. He is glad for her and cannot read her messages without his chest going tight in a way that takes hours to ease. He has not told her this. He has not told anyone most of it. He is twenty-nine and he is very tired and he is trying, in the quiet of the back room, to figure out how to live inside the life he came home to.
